Original statement: "Reasonable people will not resist the law violently, unless the consequences of resisting the law are no worse than obeying the law, thus desperate."

Let me parse this:
- "Reasonable people will not resist the law violently" - This is the main claim
- "unless the consequences of resisting the law are no worse than obeying the law" - This is the exception condition
- "thus desperate" - This seems to modify the type of resistance (desperate violent resistance)

So in logical terms:
If NOT (consequences of resisting ≤ consequences of obeying), then reasonable people will NOT resist violently.
Or equivalently:
Reasonable people will resist violently ONLY IF consequences of resisting ≤ consequences of obeying.

Now let me analyze each option:

**Option A:** "Only if the consequences of violent resistance to the law are no worse than obedience to the law, rational people will desperately and violently resist the law."

This says: Rational people will desperately violently resist the law ONLY IF consequences of resisting ≤ consequences of obeying.
This is logically equivalent to the original statement.

**Option B:** "If the consequences of violent resistance to the law are worse than obedience to the law, rational people will not desperately violently resist the law."

This says: If consequences of resisting > consequences of obeying, then rational people will NOT desperately violently resist.
This is also logically equivalent to the original (contrapositive form).

**Option C:** "If the consequences of obeying the law are better than violent resistance, the rational person will not desperately violently resist the law."

This says: If consequences of obeying > consequences of resisting, then rational person will NOT desperately violently resist.
Wait, this is actually saying: If obeying has BETTER consequences than resisting, then no violent resistance.
But the original says: Violent resistance happens ONLY IF resisting has NO WORSE consequences than obeying (i.e., resisting ≤ obeying).

Let me check: "consequences of obeying are better than violent resistance" means: obeying > resisting.
The original says violent resistance happens when resisting ≤ obeying.
So if obeying > resisting, that means resisting < obeying, which is a subset of resisting ≤ obeying.
According to the original, if resisting ≤ obeying, violent resistance CAN happen.
But Option C says if obeying > resisting (which is a case of resisting ≤ obeying), then NO violent resistance.
This contradicts the original.

**Option D:** "Only the consequences of violent resistance to the law are worse than obedience to the law. Reasonable people will not desperately violently resist the law."

This is poorly phrased but seems to say: Only if consequences of resisting > consequences of obeying, reasonable people will not desperately violently resist.
This is essentially the contrapositive of the original, so it agrees.

Wait, let me double-check Option D more carefully. "Only the consequences of violent resistance to the law are worse than obedience to the law" could mean: The ONLY case where reasonable people won't resist is when consequences of resisting > consequences of obeying.
This is: Reasonable people won't resist IF (and only if?) consequences of resisting > consequences of obeying.
The original says: Reasonable people won't resist UNLESS consequences of resisting ≤ consequences of obeying.
These are equivalent (contrapositive forms).

Actually, looking at Option D again: "Only the consequences of violent resistance to the law are worse than obedience to the law." This seems incomplete or poorly constructed. It might be saying: Only WHEN consequences of resisting are worse than obeying, reasonable people will not desperately violently resist.
That would be: If consequences of resisting > consequences of obeying, then no resistance.
This matches the original.

But Option C is clearly contradictory. Let me write the answer.
